title: U.S. Calls India a 'Critical Power' After Dropping 'Indo' From Pacific Command Name
excerpt: A senior Pentagon official pushed back against concerns that renaming INDOPACOM to PACOM signals diminished attention to India, calling the U.S.-India relationship 'vital' with 'natural partnership' potential.
body:
• The United States renamed its Indo-Pacific Command back to Pacific Command (USPACOM), reversing a 2018 decision, but a senior Pentagon official says the move does not diminish India's strategic importance.
  • Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby called India a "critical power" and said Washington seeks a stronger partnership with New Delhi.
  • The name change reflects the U.S. military's strategic focus on the Western Pacific and the first island chain, not a downgrade of the Indian Ocean region.
  • The command's area of responsibility — stretching from the U.S. West Coast to India's western border — remains unchanged.

The United States sees India as a "critical power" and wants a stronger partnership with New Delhi, a senior Pentagon official said, pushing back against concerns that the reversal of the Indo-Pacific Command name signals diminished American attention to India or the Indian Ocean.

The Name Change

The U.S. Department of War announced in June that the U.S. Indo-Pacific Command (USINDOPACOM) would revert to its original name, the U.S. Pacific Command (USPACOM). The command was first established on January 1, 1947, by President Harry Truman, and operated under the USPACOM banner for more than 70 years before being renamed in 2018 by then-Defense Secretary James Mattis.

Mattis had said the 2018 change recognized "the increasing connectivity of the Indian and Pacific Oceans" and America's commitment to the broader region. The reversal under the Trump administration's second term prompted questions about whether India and the Indian Ocean were being sidelined in U.S. strategic thinking.

Colby's Reassurance

Elbridge Colby, the Under Secretary of War for Policy, addressed those concerns directly during a virtual briefing organized by the State Department's Asia Pacific Media Hub.

"This is not in any way a sort of denigration of the importance of the Indian Ocean area or of India itself. We really see India as a critical power, and the Indian Ocean, of course, is very important."

— Elbridge Colby, Under Secretary of War for Policy

Colby said the name change reflected the U.S. military's strategic priorities as outlined in its National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy, which focus on the Western Pacific and the first island chain — the arc running from Japan through Taiwan and the Philippines toward Southeast Asia.

"The strategic focus of the United States military is really on the first island chain," Colby said. "The Pacific element to that is really the focus, the Western Pacific area, obviously stretching into Southeast Asia."

India as a "Vital Relationship"

Despite the narrower naming convention, Colby described the U.S.-India relationship as one with natural alignment. "If anything, we really see India as a vital relationship where there's a natural partnership," he said. "Let's look where our interests align. We're going to have areas where we don't always agree. But we're looking for a stronger India."

He pointed to his own visit to India in March and visits by other senior U.S. officials as evidence of continuing engagement. The command's area of responsibility — spanning from the U.S. West Coast to India's western border — remains exactly the same under the USPACOM designation.

Strategic Context

The name change is part of a broader series of rebranding initiatives at the Pentagon since the start of Trump's second term, including renaming the Department of Defense back to the Department of War. Experts and geopolitical commentators have expressed wariness about what the shift signals for India's positioning within the U.S. security architecture, particularly regarding the Quad partnership with Australia, Japan, and the United States.

Colby, speaking during a visit to the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, and Cambodia, presented the administration's regional approach as one built on military strength, practical cooperation, and respect for national sovereignty. "We're not asking for fealty; we're asking for practical things: access, collaboration, these kinds of things," he said.

What It Means for India

The reassurance from Washington comes at a time when India is deepening its own defence partnerships with the United States, including joint military exercises, defence technology transfers, and a growing arms trade. For India, the substance of the relationship — military cooperation, intelligence sharing, and strategic alignment on China — matters more than the naming convention. But the optics of dropping "Indo" from the command name have not gone unnoticed in New Delhi, where the original 2018 inclusion was seen as recognition of India's rising strategic weight.
nri_angle: The U.S.-India strategic relationship directly affects millions of Indian Americans and NRIs through defence ties, diplomatic standing, and the broader geopolitical environment in which the diaspora operates.
